baseline.what: Average dose equivalent measured on the lunar surface by the Lunar Lander Neutrons and Dosimetry (LND) experiment on China's Chang'e 4 lander (Jan-Feb 2019, solar minimum). About 2.6x the galactic-cosmic-ray dose inside the ISS.

source.title: Zhang et al. 2020, First measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface, Science Advances 6:eaaz1334
Zhang et al. 2020 (DOSIS 3D DOSTEL on the ISS, same period)

limits.what: NASA's career radiation limit for astronauts is 600 mSv.

source.title: NASA NTRS 20230012405, Biological Space Radiation Countermeasures to Enable Long Duration Exploration Missions

limits.context: Astronauts are exposed to effective doses from 50 to 2,000 mSv; 1 mSv is about 10 chest x-rays.

shielding.what: Solar-flare protons are stopped well by regolith: dose behind lunar soil drops steeply with thickness, which is why a regolith-covered storm shelter is the standard plan. Galactic cosmic rays are much harder to stop.

sources.title: NASA NTRS 19890004839, Solar-flare shielding with regolith at a lunar-base site
NASA NTRS 20110012713, Radiation shielding of lunar regolith/polyethylene composites and regolith/water mixtures

game.time_scale_note: The mission is a real 10 days. The dose numbers are scaled up so choices matter in 10 days.
game.mission_limit_note: Game limit for this one 10-day mission: 1/12 of NASA's 600 mSv career limit. Doing nothing for 10 days costs ~27 game-mSv; one big storm without shelter pushes you over.
game.shields_note: Game assumption: powered shields (water walls pumped around the crew area, plus monitoring) cut the dose rate by up to 50% at a 30% power share; effect scales linearly with share. Not a published number.
game.shelter_note: Game assumption: in the regolith-covered shelter, storm (solar particle) dose x0.25 and the steady cosmic-ray dose x0.7, reflecting that regolith stops solar protons far better than cosmic rays (NTRS 19890004839). No science or rover work happens in the shelter.
